## Marketing claims versus documented behavior

AI Dungeon’s onboarding says “anything is possible,” calls the player the “main character and director,” and says player tools help keep the AI coherent and consistent; the Memory page frames the “core promise” as freedom and meaningful choices.[1][3] These are **positioning claims**. The documented behavior is narrower: the system sends a bounded context assembled from multiple plot components, summarizes portions of history, retrieves selected memories, and acknowledges quirks and imperfect outputs.[1][2][3] The documentation therefore supports “player-directed generative storytelling with configurable context aids,” not a verified persistent world simulator or rules engine.

The strongest public limitation statements are unusually relevant to a ledger-first comparison: older text can be removed when context is exceeded; summaries can contain errors; manual correction may be required after earlier edits; longer components consume context; and the onboarding page says AI “isn’t always perfect” and may have “weird quirks.”[1][2][3] No reviewed first-party page publishes turn-50/100/200 retention, inventory accuracy, quest completion, combat fairness, contradiction rate, or image-character consistency metrics.

## Precise SynapticGM gaps/tests

A ledger-first single-player AI GM should test five separations that AI Dungeon’s public documentation leaves unresolved: **prose versus truth**, **memory versus authoritative state**, **player correction versus historical recomputation**, **safety filtering versus committed events**, and **generation cost versus state mutation**. The minimum test harness should snapshot a canonical world ledger every turn, record the exact generated text and context components, validate state deltas, and permit deterministic replay from any snapshot.

The highest-value benchmark is a 200-turn scenario with recurring NPCs, a finite inventory, currency, a multi-step quest, a combat ruleset, a retcon at turn 75, an image at turn 100, a safety-boundary prompt at turn 125, and a paid-context failure at turn 150. Pass criteria should be explicit: no impossible item counts, no duplicate entity IDs, no quest completion without prerequisites, no unseeded combat divergence, no unreviewed state mutation from filtered output, reversible corrections, and user-visible cost accounting. These are **recommended tests**, not claims about AI Dungeon’s internal implementation or measured failures.

## Marketing versus documented behavior

The homepage makes broad claims that Franz “adapts to your choices,” creates dynamic storylines, learns and uses world content “instantly,” narrates/adjudicates rules in real time, and keeps adventures moving asynchronously ([1](https://fables.gg/)). The Help Center narrows that picture: retrieval is selective and budgeted; newer/priority blocks can displace older ones; semantic long-term-memory search is less reliable; and custom instructions affect narration/output rather than mechanics or state operations ([7](https://help.fables.gg/articles/8680638-custom-instructions), [8](https://help.fables.gg/articles/8560008-working-context-blocks)). The terms further disclaim unexpected, inaccurate, omitted, or offensive outputs ([4](https://fables.gg/terms-of-service)). Accordingly, “memory,” “learns instantly,” and “adjudicates rules” should be treated as product positioning unless backed by reproducible state-level tests.

## SynapticGM implications

Friends & Fables is a relevant competitor because it combines AI GM narration, editable world/character entities, memory/context management, tactical combat, quests, maps, images, TTS, and multiplayer in one platform ([1](https://fables.gg/)). Its strongest publicly evidenced advantage for a ledger-first comparison is breadth plus user-editable entities and context. Its most important disclosed limitations are equally clear: context selection is heuristic and budgeted, long-term-memory search is less reliable, narration instructions do not control mechanics, and the service is experimental with unexpected outputs ([7](https://help.fables.gg/articles/8680638-custom-instructions), [8](https://help.fables.gg/articles/8560008-working-context-blocks), [4](https://fables.gg/terms-of-service)).

For SynapticGM, the differentiator should not be a generic claim of “better memory.” It should be **inspectable truth maintenance**: append-only event records; stable IDs for characters, items, locations, quests, and factions; explicit fact provenance and supersession; deterministic or seeded rules resolution; transactional state updates; player-visible correction with audit history; canon precedence; and export/replay at turn 50/100/200. Narrative generation should be downstream of the ledger, with context retrieval exposing citations to the exact authoritative records used. This directly addresses the public gaps identified above without claiming that Friends & Fables fails in every case.

Priority benchmark suite: (1) a 200-turn inventory/economy conservation test; (2) recurring-NPC identity and relationship test; (3) canon conflict and correction test; (4) seeded combat/replay test; (5) branch-locked quest test; (6) context-budget recall test; and (7) transparent metering, refund, deletion, privacy, and safety test. Results should report reproducible transcripts, ledger diffs, retrieved sources, and failure severity rather than anecdotal prose quality.

The defensible conclusion is **architecture/design intent publicly asserted, operational reliability unverified**.

## Precise ledger-first tests for SynapticGM

SynapticGM should test Hidden Door-like claims with a canonical event ledger and replay oracle rather than judging prose alone. First, run a **200-turn entity invariant test**: create two NPCs, three locations, five items, explicit ownership and quantities, then alternate travel, trade, consume, destroy, and rename actions. At turns 50, 100, and 200, compare narrated facts against a canonical snapshot; every contradiction must be classified as a presentation error, rejected transition, or committed state error.

Second, run **modifier precedence and rollback tests**. Apply a base rule, two modifiers with conflicting tone/rules, and a player correction; verify that the system exposes which rule wins, records the decision as an event, supports a deterministic replay, and can roll back only the disputed event without deleting unrelated progress. Hidden Door publicly documents modifiers and world rules but not precedence or rollback.[1]

Third, run an **NPC truth and relationship test**. Give each NPC immutable identity, goals, secrets, relationship edges, and changing beliefs; force contradictory player assertions over 200 turns. The GM should distinguish “player claim,” “NPC belief,” and “world fact,” preserve provenance, and offer a correction path rather than silently canonizing the latest prose.

Fourth, run a **quest lifecycle test** across multiple short stories: create an objective with prerequisites, partial progress, failure, abandonment, and re-entry. Verify that scene/story boundaries do not reset progress, that rewards are idempotent, and that completed objectives cannot be reopened without an explicit event. The public Hidden Door documentation describes story endings and replay but does not document quest persistence semantics.[1]

Fifth, run **fairness and explainability tests** with fixed seeds and hidden versus visible difficulty. Repeat equivalent actions under identical state, record dice outcomes and modifiers, and require an after-action explanation that cites the ledger state used. If the product intentionally hides numbers, provide at least a player-readable reason code and a correction/escalation mechanism.

Sixth, run **safety and cost boundary tests** using age-appropriate, Mature-labeled, sexual-content, self-harm, harassment, and prompt-injection cases. Verify world-level maturity settings, warnings, refusal/fade-to-black behavior, logging, and no cross-world leakage. Separately test free-to-paid upgrade, cancellation, renewal, private/unlisted access, and payout attribution with a ledger of entitlements and payments; assert that stories and progress remain available exactly as publicly promised.[2][4][5]

## Bottom line

Hidden Door’s public materials describe a **human-authored, card/deck-mediated interactive story system with structured world/entity state, light probabilistic rules, remixable modifiers, creator worldbuilding, sparse hand-drawn art, and a subscription model that avoids pay-per-turn interruptions**.[1][2] Its public trust posture is comparatively explicit about age thresholds, content restrictions, generated-output fallibility, third-party processing, retention, and the limits of security.[4][5] For SynapticGM, the key competitive gap is not the existence of cards or an AI narrator; it is **verifiable state authority**: inspectable provenance, deterministic replay, explicit conflict resolution, player correction, and long-horizon invariants. Those mechanisms are not documented in the reviewed public pages and should be treated as the principal audit and product-differentiation test surface.

## Marketing claims versus documented behavior

The homepage/FAQ uses expansive positioning such as “unprecedented level of freedom,” “limitless playground,” and “AI driven anime image generator and storytelling tool.” [5](https://docs.novelai.net/en/faq/) The product pages call the image tooling “powerful creative tools” and advertise the latest model and free-trial access. [7](https://novelai.net/image) These are marketing or positioning claims, not measured guarantees of consistency, factuality, fairness, quest completion, or safety.

By contrast, the documentation makes narrower, testable statements: Memory and Author’s Note are injected into context; Lorebook entries activate based on keys and can be constrained by budgets and conditions; context can trim or exclude content; users can inspect the assembled context; Opus has a stated maximum context size; image history is session-based unless saved; and subscription/image-credit rules are specified. [1](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/storysettings/) [2](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/lorebook/) [3](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/advancedsettings/) [5](https://docs.novelai.net/en/faq/) [8](https://docs.novelai.net/en/subscription/)

## Turn-50-to-200 failure-mode inferences

The following are **inferences for audit design, not verified NovelAI behavior**. They follow from the documented reliance on finite context, manually updated Memory/Author’s Note, key-triggered Lorebook activation, token budgets/trimming, and probabilistic generation. [2](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/lorebook/) [3](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/advancedsettings/) [4](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/glossary/)

| Inferred long-horizon risk | Why it is plausible | Ledger-first implication |
|---|---|---|
| Canon drift or duplicated facts | A fact may be absent from the active context, while Lorebook activation depends on exact/regex-like keys and recent search windows. | Every authoritative fact should live in a structured ledger and be checked before narration, not merely restated in prose or Memory. |
| Inventory loss, duplication, or ownership confusion | Lorebook documents narrative entries but not atomic item transactions or uniqueness/quantity constraints. | Test acquire/use/drop/transfer/stack/split and verify conservation after 50, 100, and 200 turns. |
| Quest soft-lock or false completion | No reviewed source documents quest state, prerequisites, proof conditions, or rollback semantics. | Require explicit objective IDs, prerequisite evaluation, completion evidence, and replayable state diffs. |
| Combat fairness drift | Random/numeric conditions are documented for lore activation, not a complete audited combat engine. | Test seeded outcomes, legal action validation, hidden-information handling, and invariant checks against a reference resolver. |
| Personality/style erosion | Style is steered with modules, tags, presets, notes, and biases, but no persistence guarantee is stated. | Separate style/persona regression tests from world-state correctness tests; score both at fixed checkpoints. |
| Contradictory correction propagation | Manual edits affect context inputs, but the docs do not claim automatic repair of prior prose, lore entries, or generated images. | A correction must create a versioned ledger event and invalidate/recompute dependent projections. |
| Context-budget starvation | Documentation explicitly says entries and story text can cancel one another and be trimmed/excluded as context is built. | Log the exact context sent to the model and fail closed when required state is omitted. |
| Visual/text mismatch | Image references and character prompts are documented, but no automatic binding to item/character ledger state is documented. | Generate visuals from a canonical snapshot and test equipment, color, injury, and location consistency. |
| Cost surprise at scale | Image generation consumes Anlas except under stated conditions, and tier/context/refill rules differ. [8](https://docs.novelai.net/en/subscription/) | Estimate and display per-action cost before generation; test renewal, cancellation, paid-versus-subscription Anlas, and failed-generation behavior. |
| Recoverability failure | Remote content is encrypted and password/email loss can block access; deleted stories are documented as unrecoverable. [1](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/storysettings/) [5](https://docs.novelai.net/en/faq/) | Provide portable, versioned, human-readable ledger exports and restore tests independent of provider account recovery. |

## Precise gaps and tests for a ledger-first single-player AI GM

| Gap to resolve | Proposed test and acceptance evidence |
|---|---|
| No public proof of authoritative state | Run a 200-turn scripted campaign with hidden ledger state; compare every narrated claim against the ledger and require zero unauthorized mutations. |
| No documented transaction semantics | Test item and currency conservation across acquire, consume, sell, steal, trade, death, reload, undo, and branch merge; require append-only event records and deterministic replay. |
| No documented correction protocol | Inject corrections at turns 50, 100, and 150; verify the system records who/when/why, updates dependent quests/NPC attitudes, and prevents stale projections from resurfacing. |
| No documented quest model | Use branching objectives with optional, mutually exclusive, timed, and failed states; require explicit IDs, prerequisites, completion evidence, and explainable status. |
| No documented combat/rules fairness | Replay identical seeds and inputs; compare outcomes to a reference rules engine; test impossible actions, adversarial prompts, random distribution, and save/reload determinism. |
| Context inclusion is observable but not guaranteed | Capture context viewer/context payload at each checkpoint; verify all required ledger summaries are included within budget, never silently trimmed, and trigger a visible failure when not. |
| No long-run persona guarantee | Use a fixed persona rubric at turns 1/50/100/200 and adversarially prompt personality flips; require bounded variance or explicit player override behavior. |
| No image-canon binding | Generate character/equipment/location images from ledger snapshots at checkpoints; compare against structured attributes and require a mismatch warning rather than silent invention. |
| Cost and safety boundaries need product-specific validation | Test free-trial exhaustion, tier upgrades/downgrades, cancellation, Anlas depletion, tax/renewal presentation, adult-age gate, sexual/violent content boundaries, and export after subscription termination using the live UI and Terms as the oracle. |

**Bottom line for SynapticGM:** NovelAI publicly demonstrates a mature **manual context orchestration and creative-generation toolkit**, including inspectable context, Lorebook retrieval, adjustable budgets, correction controls, story branching/export, and image references. [1](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/storysettings/) [2](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/lorebook/) [3](https://docs.novelai.net/en/text/editor/advancedsettings/) It does not publicly establish the core trust proposition of a single-player AI GM: a canonical, transactional, replayable ledger that adjudicates rules and prevents state drift over 50–200 turns. SynapticGM should therefore compete on **state authority, explicit provenance, correction/replay, deterministic or auditable rules, and cost/safety transparency**, while treating NovelAI’s controllable context and broad style/image tooling as the relevant benchmark rather than assuming those controls equal game-state correctness.

| Gap to resolve | Test protocol | Pass condition for a ledger-first single-player AI GM |
|---|---|---|

Overall, Quest Portal publicly documents a capable **AI-assisted VTT and GM-preparation workflow**, with strong support for editable sheets, notes, maps, source/PDF lookup, and player/GM session separation. [Homepage](https://www.questportal.com/) [Assistant](https://www.questportal.com/assistant) The principal competitive gap for SynapticGM is not breadth of creative tooling; it is demonstrable **state integrity**: an inspectable, ledger-first truth model that governs inventory, quests, combat, canon, corrections, provenance, privacy boundaries, and cost before narrative fluency is considered.

## Cost-model implications for a ledger-first GM

The public benchmark baseline is **tiered, usage-metered model access plus product-level quotas**, not a reliable fixed-cost game service. OpenAI exposes materially different standard, cached, batch, flex, fast, and long-context prices; Anthropic similarly exposes base, cache-write, cache-hit, output, cloud-platform, and regional pricing distinctions.[1][7] This makes a ledger-first architecture economically important: the system should keep canonical state compact and structured, retrieve only relevant slices, cache immutable campaign rules, and route narration separately from expensive adjudication. That is an architectural implication, not a claim that either vendor recommends SynapticGM’s design.

A practical public-cost test should record, for every turn, model, input tokens, cached tokens, output tokens, tool calls, image/audio calls, latency tier, retries, and monetary estimate. Report median and p95 cost for turns 1–50, 51–100, and 101–200 under identical scenarios. A fair comparison must state whether the transcript is resent, whether a structured ledger replaces transcript history, whether cache hits are available, and whether image generation is included. Without those controls, “cheap” and “long-context” comparisons are not comparable.

## Precise gaps and acceptance tests for SynapticGM

SynapticGM should not benchmark itself only on prose quality. It should publish a **state-integrity suite** with: (1) exact inventory and currency conservation; (2) unique IDs for characters, items, locations, quests, and effects; (3) append-only event records with turn number and causal links; (4) explicit player-correction operations; (5) canonical-source precedence and unsupported-fact refusal; (6) deterministic or seed-replayable combat; (7) quest dependency and completion checks; (8) safety refusal without state mutation; and (9) per-turn token/cost accounting.

The key public-service comparison is therefore: do not ask whether a model “has memory.” Ask whether the service exposes enough control for SynapticGM to implement **authoritative state outside the model**, how much retrieval/context costs at turns 50–200, and whether the model can reliably render that state without inventing or mutating it. The reviewed public pages support using model services as narrators/reasoners with project/context features, but they do not evidence a complete ledger-first single-player AI GM.
